cues.text: A Miraculous Birth Foretold

John's birth was announced by the angel Gabriel to his father, the priest Zechariah, while he was serving in the Jerusalem Temple — a birth so unlikely, given that Zechariah's wife Elizabeth was already advanced in years and had long been childless, that Zechariah's own doubt at the news left him struck mute until the child was born.

When Mary , newly pregnant with Jesus, visited her cousin Elizabeth, the unborn John is recorded as having leapt in his mother's womb at Mary's greeting, and Elizabeth herself, filled with the Holy Spirit, cried out in recognition of the child Mary carried — the very first, wordless recognition, before either child had drawn breath outside the womb, of the relationship between the Forerunner and the One he had been sent to announce.
A Prophet's Naming

At John's circumcision, relatives assumed he would be named after his father, but Elizabeth insisted he be called John, and when the still-mute Zechariah confirmed this in writing, his own speech was restored, and he burst into prophecy, blessing God for raising up a Savior and declaring of his own infant son that he would be called the prophet of the Most High, going before the Lord to prepare his ways — the canticle known ever since as the Benedictus , still prayed each morning in the Church's Liturgy of the Hours.
A Voice in the Wilderness

John grew up, Scripture tells us only briefly, in the desert, and emerged as an adult preaching a baptism of repentance for the forgiveness of sins along the banks of the Jordan River , dressed in a rough garment of camel's hair and living on locusts and wild honey — an appearance and manner of life deliberately reminiscent of the ancient prophet Elijah, whom many of his contemporaries believed he might in some sense embody.

Crowds came from Jerusalem and the whole surrounding countryside to hear him and be baptized, confessing their sins, and John's preaching, blunt and uncompromising, spared no one — not the religious leaders he called a "brood of vipers," nor, eventually, the ruling king himself.
"I Must Decrease"

When Jesus himself came to be baptized, John recognized him immediately and protested that their roles ought to be reversed, that it was he who needed baptism from Jesus rather than the other way around — yielding only when Jesus insisted it was fitting, for the moment, to fulfill all righteousness in this way.

John's own disciples later expressed some concern as crowds increasingly followed Jesus rather than their own master, and John's response remains one of the most luminous statements of humility in the entire Gospel: he must increase, but I must decrease — a forerunner's clear-eyed recognition that his entire mission existed only to point beyond himself.
Speaking Truth to a King

John's fearless preaching eventually turned to public rebuke of Herod Antipas , the regional ruler, for unlawfully taking his own brother's wife, Herodias, as his own — a denunciation that led to John's imprisonment, since Herod, though troubled and even fascinated by John's preaching, did not at first dare to kill a man so widely regarded by the people as a genuine prophet.

Herodias, however, harbored a deeper grudge, and found her opportunity at a lavish birthday banquet, when her daughter's dance so pleased Herod that he rashly swore to grant her any request — a promise Herodias exploited, through her daughter, to demand the immediate execution of John and the delivery of his head on a platter.
A Martyr's Death
Herod, trapped by his own public oath before his assembled guests, reluctantly ordered John's execution, and the great prophet who had baptized the Messiah himself was beheaded in prison.

Even from his cell before this final act, John had continued to bear witness, sending his own disciples to ask Jesus directly whether he was indeed the one who was to come — a question Jesus answered not with a simple yes, but by pointing to the very signs of the kingdom already unfolding around him, the blind seeing and the lame walking, entrusting John, even in doubt, with evidence rather than mere assertion.
Legacy
Christ's own assessment of John remains one of the highest tributes given to any human being in the Gospels: that among those born of women, none had arisen greater than John the Baptist.

The last and greatest of the Old Testament prophets, and the first to point directly at Christ as "the Lamb of God who takes away the sins of the world," John stands at the exact hinge between two covenants — a voice whose entire life and death were oriented, without reservation, toward preparing the way for someone greater than himself, a model of self-emptying witness the Church has never ceased to honor.
